Let me explain: 1) You have the majority of people in the US with little to no serious health conditions, who paid for insurance plans or had it through work. Because they're low risk (or pooled risk through a company), their insurance is cheap. Copays are low, and if you want to do an HSA and a catastrophic plan, its really cheap. When the ACA is passed, 2 things happen. The requirements for what plans have to cover increases and include things people don't necessarily want or need, increasing the cost of each plan. Second, risk stratification is banned, so you aren't actually buying insurance anymore, you're buying healthcare plans that don't take your health into account. The government literally took away your right to buy an insurance plan based on the your health. Ok, so now, plans are way more expensive (I could get a great plan as a young healthy person for $100/mo, now I pay twice that with a higher deductible). Immediately, this rate increase is going to price people out of plans, or force them to go to the healthcare marketplace (but we'll get to that in a minute).

2) You have the small minority of people who have serious chronic health conditions and cannot afford coverage. They couldn't afford or couldn't get coverage previously, and now can because all of their costs get passed to everyone else. I'm not actually sure what to do with these people, and personally I don't think I would be against having Medicaid or a government plan cover them. What I do not believe is that the government should force citizens to pay companies to cover other people's health problems. Since the ACA was passed, these people can now get coverage through the marketplace, and their care will be expensive, but still covered.

3) There is now a huge third group of people created by the ACA, those who think they have insurance, but don't because they won't be able to afford it if anything happens to them. The marketplace plans come with crazy high deductibles. They're basically so high that they would have been considered catastrophic plans before the ACA. If a person with low income (a huge percentage of those with marketplace plans) were to get very sick and require a hospital stay or surgery, they would be responsible for paying up to their multi-thousand dollar deductible. In most cases, they won't be able to pay. Aside from their yearly checkup they get for free, these plans are just going to bleed them dry. I won't even get started on how difficult it is to find doctors that actually take marketplace plans. These are the ones who go to the ER every time they get sick.

So, my point is, you've got two very large groups who now have more difficulty affording their healthcare. Those who are healthy and have seen huge rate increases under the ACA, and those who bought cheap marketplace plans, but actually can't find a doctor, and will still be on the hook for thousands if anything happens. There is one smaller group that benefits, those who had serious chronic conditions, and can now buy plans subsidized by literally everyone else. I'm not sure how to fix the system. I know that I single payer system could work, and with the amount we pay for healthcare in the US, we could have a single payer system that far surpasses anything in the rest of the world. We should also remember that the insurance market is not a free market. It is highly regulated, and that prevents good competition. Instituting a safety net for those who can't get insurance on the free market, but allowing strong interstate competition would also get us a system that far surpasses what we have now.

Note: I'm a 4th year medical student who will be a practicing physician in a few months time.
